questions.q: What are the three responsibilities the lesson says must be separated into different modules in a quantum package?
options: Circuit construction, backend execution, and result analysis
Qubits, gates, and measurements
Python files, YAML files, and JSON files
Unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests
questions.explain: The lesson identifies circuit construction, execution/backend, and result analysis as three distinct responsibilities that cause real problems when mixed in one module -- untestable circuit logic, backend lock-in, and un-reusable analysis code.

questions.q: Why does mixing circuit-building and `.run()` in the same function make unit testing harder?
options: It doesn't -- unit tests work the same either way
Because verifying the circuit's gate sequence then secretly requires actually executing it, turning every 'unit test' into an integration test dependent on a backend
Because Qiskit refuses to import functions that call .run()
Because pytest cannot import files with more than one function
questions.explain: If building and running are fused together, you can't check gate sequence or qubit wiring without executing the circuit on some backend -- making the test an integration test, and vulnerable to backend flakiness, rather than a fast, deterministic unit test.

questions.q: Where does the lesson recommend putting noise models and default shot counts, and why?
options: Hardcoded as Python constants inside the circuit module, for speed
In a config/ directory as YAML or JSON, since they change more often and differ between environments than circuit logic does
Inside the pytest configuration file only
They should never be stored anywhere and always passed as hardcoded literals
questions.explain: Noise models and shot counts vary between laptop, CI, and production hardware runs far more than circuit logic does, so the lesson recommends externalizing them into config files rather than hardcoding them into .py modules.

questions.q: What has replaced `setup.py` as the modern standard for configuring an installable Python package, and what does the lesson's example pin exactly rather than with a loose range?
options: requirements.txt; it pins Python itself
pyproject.toml; it pins the quantum SDK versions (e.g. qiskit==1.2.4) with ==
Pipfile; it pins only the test framework
conda.yaml; it pins the operating system
questions.explain: pyproject.toml is the modern standard packaging file. The example deliberately uses == exact pins for qiskit and qiskit-aer rather than >= ranges, because quantum SDKs need tighter version control than most classical dependencies (explained further in Chapter 4).

questions.q: In the example grover-toolkit layout, which directory is specifically responsible for turning raw measurement counts into a statistical verdict, reusable across different algorithms?
options: circuits/
backends/
analysis/
config/
questions.explain: analysis/statistics.py is where the lesson places the counts-to-verdict statistical testing logic (built out fully in Chapter 2), specifically because that logic is the same regardless of which algorithm produced the counts.
